pedagogy.summary: Year 2 sharpens the movement vocabulary: children add clockwise and anti-clockwise to whole, half, quarter and three-quarter turns, link a quarter turn to a right angle, and give and follow multi-step directions combining straight-line moves with turns. The words are to be used, not defined — the aim is fluent, correct use in routes and turn descriptions. Clockwise/anti-clockwise is a new convention layered onto the still-developing left/right, and the quarter-turn = right-angle link is the crucial bridge to the formal angle work that follows.
bestPractices: Introduce clockwise from a real clock's hands, then transfer it to the body and to turning objects, contrasting it explicitly with anti-clockwise each time.
Make the quarter-turn = right-angle link concrete: turn a quarter and mark the right angle between the start and finish arms (an angle is an amount of turn shown by two adjoining lines).
Combine moves and turns into routes to give and follow (barrier games, floor robots) so the vocabulary is productive.
Keep turns embodied and referenced to target facings before moving to described or drawn routes.
Continue supporting left/right on the body and expect residual errors as frame-dependence is still developing.
keyRepresentations: A clock face for clockwise and anti-clockwise
Body or floor-robot turns with start/finish facings, and the right-angle mark left by a quarter turn
Route maps and grids to describe and to follow with combined moves and turns
Two adjoining arms (the start and finish of a turn) showing the angle turned through
commonMisconceptions: Clockwise and anti-clockwise confused with each other or with left/right — a new convention on top of frame-dependent left/right
A quarter turn not connected to a right angle — the two treated as separate, unrelated facts
Turn amounts miscounted — a half or a quarter turn produced when a three-quarter turn is asked for
Egocentric direction-giving: routes given from the child's own viewpoint without accounting for the follower's facing

learn.summary: Year 2 children use (not merely define) movement vocabulary: clockwise and anti-clockwise added to whole, half, quarter and three-quarter turns; a quarter turn linked to a right angle; and multi-step directions combining straight-line moves with turns that another person can actually follow. Clockwise/anti-clockwise is a new convention layered on still-developing left/right, and the quarter-turn = right-angle link bridges to later formal angle work. Guidance keeps turns embodied and routes followable, with feedback on wrong direction or amount.

activities.title: Clockwise, anti-clockwise and the right angle a quarter turn leaves
feedback: If a child turns the wrong way on a clockwise/anti-clockwise instruction, return to a real clock's hand direction as the anchor and label both ways explicitly each time.
If a child makes the quarter turn but cannot name or denies the right angle, mark the right angle between the start and finish arms every single time until the link becomes automatic.
When a child miscounts the turn amount (e.g. a half or quarter turn when a three-quarter turn was asked), count the quarter turns aloud — one, two, three — marking each right angle as it is passed.
Confirm when two clockwise quarter turns are recognised as a half turn, reinforcing that quarters accumulate.
activities.rationale: The curriculum expects pupils to distinguish rotation as a turn and in terms of right angles for quarter, half and three-quarter turns, clockwise and anti-clockwise. An angle is an amount of turn shown by two adjoining lines, and the dynamic (turn) and static (corner) conceptions of a right angle must be brought together, which marking the arms of a quarter turn supports. A manipulable clock/dial with a stamped right angle makes the mechanism concrete; a fixed diagram can still illustrate the link but cannot be turned by the child.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils should use mathematical vocabulary to describe position, direction and movement, including movement in a straight line and distinguishing between rotation as a turn and in terms of right angles for quarter, half and three-quarter turns (clockwise and anti-clockwise).

An angle is an amount of turn represented by two adjoining lines (start and finish positions); children develop right angles as quarter turns by turning with one arm fixed while the other moves, linking turn to the right angle formed — the static (corner) and dynamic (turn) conceptions must come together.
learnerActions: Watch a real clock's hands and name the direction they travel as 'clockwise'; then turn your own body a quarter turn clockwise (towards your right, the way the hands would go on a clock lying face-up on the floor and seen from above) and say where you now face.
Make a quarter turn clockwise and mark or point out the corner (angle) between where you started facing and where you finish facing; name it as a right angle.
Make the same quarter turn anti-clockwise and describe how the finishing facing differs.

On a clock face or turn dial, spin an arrow with a 'clockwise, quarter turn' control so it moves 90° and leaves a right-angle mark between start and finish; use 'anti-clockwise' to send it back the other way.
Make two quarter turns clockwise in a row and decide whether that equals one half turn, counting each quarter aloud.
Make a three-quarter turn clockwise, counting the quarters, and point out that three right angles have been passed.
activities.intendedInsight: A quarter turn always leaves a right angle between the start and finish arms, and clockwise versus anti-clockwise decides which way you turn — turning fuzzy words into exact instructions.

activities.title: Give and follow a multi-step route that someone else can act on
feedback: If a child gives directions from their own viewpoint so 'turn left' is wrong for the follower, do NOT treat it as a failure: walk the route exactly as they said so they SEE the mismatch, then model taking the follower's view. De-centring matures with age.
When a robot hits a wall, name whether the direction or the amount of turn was wrong and let the child re-string the instruction.
Probe with 'turn that quarter anti-clockwise this time — where do you face now?' to check the direction convention under a new turn.
Ask 'when you say turn left, is that your left or mine?' to surface the follower's frame of reference.
activities.rationale: Giving and following directions that combine straight-line movement and turns makes the vocabulary productive rather than merely recognised. Left/right and route-taking are frame-dependent and late-developing; young children are egocentric and find it hard to imagine a route from another's viewpoint, so making the follower act it out literally is a developmental support, not a test to pass. Immediate feedback on wrong direction or amount (a wall, a mismatch walked out) ties the words to consequences.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils should use mathematical vocabulary to describe position, direction and movement, including movement in a straight line and distinguishing between rotation as a turn and in terms of right angles for quarter, half and three-quarter turns (clockwise and anti-clockwise).

Left and right are frame-dependent (relative to the direction the child faces) and late-developing; young children are egocentric and find it hard to de-center and imagine how a space or route looks from another point of view, which they master only as they get older.
learnerActions: Guide a partner (or a floor robot) from one point to another using a sequence such as 'forward 2, turn clockwise quarter, forward 3', combining straight-line moves with named turns.
Have the follower act out the route exactly as given, from the follower's own facing, and watch what happens.
On a grid, drive a programmable robot through a maze by stringing moves and turns; a wrong turn direction or wrong amount sends it into a wall, prompting a correction.
Play a barrier game: describe a route to someone who cannot see your map, using direction and turn words precisely enough for them to reproduce it.
When a route 'goes wrong', revise the instructions so the follower, not just you, can reach the target.
activities.intendedInsight: Direction and turn words are most useful when they form a sequence another person can follow from their own viewpoint — producing a followable route is the real goal.

activities.title: Check and sort turn and route language
feedback: If a selection is wrong, re-make the turn physically and compare the finishing facing.
For a mismatched quarter-turn/right-angle pairing, mark the angle between start and finish arms and compare.
Treat recognition choices as a check only; always follow with giving or following a live route so the child constructs instructions, not just identifies them.
activities.rationale: Selecting a facing, matching a quarter turn to a right angle, and sequencing a route give a reliable, quick check of the vocabulary. Such recognition tasks confirm what a child can identify but do not by themselves elicit the child's own construction of turns and routes, so they supplement rather than replace the embodied and productive activities above.
learnerActions: After a stated clockwise or anti-clockwise quarter turn, pick which direction you now face from given options.
Match a quarter turn to one right angle, a half turn to two right angles, and a three-quarter turn to three right angles.
Put a jumbled set of move-and-turn instructions into the order that reaches a target, then test the order by walking or driving it.
activities.intendedInsight: You can recognise correct turn facings and the quarter-turn/right-angle link quickly, then confirm sequences by acting them out.

constraints: The goal is fluent, correct USE of the words in routes and turn descriptions, not reciting definitions.
Keep turns embodied and referenced to target facings before moving to described or drawn routes.
Introduce clockwise from a real clock's hands, then transfer to the body and to turning objects, contrasting it explicitly with anti-clockwise each time.
Continue supporting left/right on the body and expect residual errors: frame-dependence is still developing at this age.
Egocentric direction-giving is developmentally expected, not a failure; surface it by having the follower act the route out literally rather than correcting abstractly.

Recognition/selection and matching tasks can check the vocabulary but do not by themselves elicit the child producing turns and followable routes, so the child must still construct turns and routes themselves.

A fixed picture or diagram can illustrate the quarter-turn/right-angle link but cannot be turned by the child; a manipulable dial or embodied turn supplies the dynamic experience. Neither claim is that a static image 'cannot teach' the idea.

Interactive controls (clockwise/anti-clockwise and quarter/half buttons, a stamped right-angle mark, a robot that hits a wall on a wrong move) are optional ways to make feedback concrete, not required mechanisms.
Rendering turns and routes in 3D is optional; the ideas are planar and do not require it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: a quarter turn = one right angle (90°); two quarter turns = one half turn (180°) = two right angles; a three-quarter turn = three right angles. These were checked and are correct. The three-quarter-turn mis-count example (producing a half or quarter instead) is retained as an error pattern, not taught as correct.

The original source row rated open conversation as a 'poor' fit and framed a recognition/selection artefact as assessing 'without building the doing'; these are framed here as scope limits (recognition does not by itself elicit construction) rather than universal claims that dialogue or static media cannot teach.

Legacy comparative framing ('a static picture cannot deliver', '3D adds little') has been softened to stated affordances/limits without asserting new efficacy comparisons, since the exact sources do not establish necessity or comparative effectiveness.

probeDeeper: Do that turn again but anti-clockwise this time — where do you face now?
You turned a quarter. Show me the corner you made between where you started and where you're facing — what kind of angle is that?
Make two quarter turns clockwise — is that the same as a half turn?
I'm going to actually follow your directions from where I'm standing — when you say 'turn left', is that your left or mine?
assess.correctAnswer: Turns the correct direction for clockwise, names the quarter turn as a right angle, and gives the route as a followable sequence using correct directional and turn vocabulary — adjusted so that the follower, not just the child, can act on it.

errorPatterns.pattern: Turns anti-clockwise when told clockwise (or treats the two as the same) — the new convention not yet stable ('clockwise... this way?')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to a real clock's hand direction as the anchor and label both ways explicitly each time.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Turns the wrong direction on a clockwise or anti-clockwise instruction

errorPatterns.pattern: Does not link a quarter turn to a right angle — treats 'quarter turn' and 'right angle' as unrelated
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mark the right angle between the start and finish arms of the quarter turn every single time until the link is automatic.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Makes a quarter turn but cannot name the angle turned through, or denies that it is a right angle

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts the turn amount — produces a half or a quarter turn when a three-quarter turn is asked for
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the quarter turns aloud (one, two, three), marking each right angle as it is passed.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The finish facing after the requested turn is wrong

errorPatterns.pattern: Gives directions from own viewpoint without adjusting for the follower's facing, so 'turn left' is wrong for the person following
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT treat as a failure — walk it exactly as they said so they SEE the mismatch, and model taking the follower's view; de-centring matures with age.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When you follow their route exactly from your own facing, the turns come out wrong

responseLevels.gap: Confuses clockwise and anti-clockwise, does not link a quarter turn to a right angle, and gives unfollowable or purely egocentric routes.
responseLevels.full: Uses clockwise / anti-clockwise and quarter / half / three-quarter turns correctly, names a quarter turn as a right angle, and gives and follows multi-step routes combining moves and turns that another person can act on, transferring to new routes (relational) — beginning to adjust for the follower's viewpoint.
responseLevels.partial: Uses quarter and half turns and follows single instructions, and can echo clockwise and right-angle language, but turns the wrong way on clockwise/anti-clockwise, does not spontaneously name the quarter turn as a right angle, or gives routes only from their own viewpoint (multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give a context and listen for USE: 'Face the window. Make a quarter turn clockwise — which way did you go, and what is the angle you turned through? ... Now guide me from the door to your chair, telling me every move and every turn.' Listen for correct use of clockwise / anti-clockwise, quarter / half / three-quarter, right angle, and a route someone could actually follow.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Combining clockwise with a turn amount, then requiring the right-angle naming and a followable route, separates a child who uses the vocabulary as precise instructions from one who parrots the words but turns the wrong way, omits the right-angle link, or gives an egocentric route. Producing a route the teacher can actually follow is the discriminator.
